title: You're Not a Universal Mosquito Magnet
gist: Florida International University researchers tested 119 people against three disease-carrying U.S. mosquito species to identify what skin microbiome and odor compounds make certain individuals especially attractive to specific species.

insights.claim: Of more than 3,500 known mosquito species worldwide, only a handful seek out human blood, and all of the disease-carrying species that target humans in the U.S.—Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus (dengue, Zika, yellow fever), and Culex quinquefasciatus (West Nile virus)—are among them.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Establishes the narrow set of disease-relevant mosquito species (out of 3,500+) driving U.S. public-health vector concerns for dengue, Zika, yellow fever, and West Nile virus.
insights.quote: out of more than 3,500 mosquito species, only a handful actually seek us out...Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus carry dengue, Zika, and yellow fever, while Culex quinquefasciatus can pass on West Nile Virus

insights.claim: A study published in iScience, led by Florida International University scientists, recruited 119 people to place their arms in mosquito-filled mesh-screened tubes, then identified the most and least attractive individuals to each of the three species and sampled their skin microbiome and odor-causing volatile compounds.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Describes the specific experimental method (n=119, arm-in-tube exposure test) used to isolate biological drivers of individual mosquito attractiveness by species.
insights.quote: A team led by scientists at Florida International University recruited 119 people willing to stick their arms inside a mosquito-filled tube...and vigorously swabbed their skin to sample both their microbiome and any odor-causing volatile compounds
